title: Protecting the Environment
text:
Many people say that they care about the environment, but caring is not always enough. Factories damage the environment when they put waste into rivers, and cars harm it by producing fumes. Scientists warn that environmental problems such as air pollution and climate change affect people in every country, not only in big industrial cities. For example, a single large factory can pollute the air over a whole town for many years. Even a small town can suffer if its rubbish is not collected.

Governments can improve the environment by making strict laws. In many countries, a factory has to pay a large fine if it pollutes a river. National parks protect the natural environment, because nobody is allowed to build houses or roads there. Some cities have also introduced zones in the centre where the oldest and dirtiest cars cannot enter.

However, laws are not the only answer. Individuals can make a difference, too. People can use public transport, recycle paper and plastic, and buy environmentally friendly products. The author believes that environmental protection begins at home, and that small daily choices are as important as government decisions.

title: Looking for a Job
text:
Finding a job is rarely easy. Most people have to apply for several jobs before somebody offers them one. The first step is a good CV: it should be short, clear and honest. Employers often receive hundreds of CVs for a single job vacancy, so they spend only a minute or two on each one. A short, tidy CV with no spelling mistakes usually makes a better impression than a long one.

If you are invited for an interview, preparation is important. You should find out about the company, think about the questions that the interviewer may ask and arrive early. Interviewers do not only want to see your skills; they also want to know if you will fit into their team.

Not everybody wants a full-time job. Some people prefer a part-time job, because it gives them time to study or to look after children. Others choose a well-paid job in a big company, but then find out that they have no job satisfaction. The writer believes that a good job is not only about money. It is also about doing a job that you enjoy and that makes you feel useful.

title: The Package Holiday
text:
Forty years ago, most people went on holiday to a place near their home. Today, millions of people take a holiday abroad every year, and the package holiday is one of the reasons. When you book a package holiday, the price usually includes the flight, the hotel and the transfer from the airport. This makes it cheap and easy, because you do not have to organise everything yourself.

For families with small children, package holidays can be a good choice. Holiday resorts often have swimming pools, children's clubs and restaurants in the same place. Parents can relax, and nobody has to worry about getting lost in a foreign city.

On the other hand, some travellers say that package holidays are boring. They complain that all resorts look the same and that tourists never meet local people. Many young people now prefer to plan their own trip: they book a cheap flight, sleep in small guesthouses and travel from town to town. The article suggests that the best choice depends on your age, your budget and the kind of experience that you want.

title: Free Education for Everyone?
text:
In many countries, children receive a free state education from the age of five or six. Primary education usually lasts for about six years, and secondary education for another five or six. In most places, the government pays for the teachers, the buildings and often the textbooks. In many places, children must go to school until the age of sixteen.

Higher education is different. A university education is expensive in some countries, and students often take a loan to pay for it. After they graduate, they may spend ten or twenty years paying the money back. Supporters of free university education argue that society needs doctors, engineers and teachers, and that talented people should not be stopped by money. Opponents say that the taxpayers should not pay for the studies of people who will earn high salaries later.

Adult education is also growing. More and more people return to evening classes to learn a new skill or change their career. The author believes that education does not end with a diploma: a modern education system should help people to learn at every age.

title: Sport for Life
text:
Doctors say that everybody should do sport, but many adults stop playing when they leave school. One reason is time. Another reason is that they think they are not good enough. In fact, you do not need to be good at sport to enjoy it. Many people take up a new sport at the age of forty or fifty, and they become keen on running, swimming or cycling. Doctors add that it is never too late to start.

Team sports have an extra advantage: they teach people to cooperate. A child who plays football or volleyball learns to listen to other players and to accept a defeat. These lessons are useful not only in sport, but also in school and at work. Individual sports, such as tennis or swimming, develop discipline, because the athlete has to train alone.

Watching sport on TV is also popular, but experts warn that it is not the same as playing. A person who spends five hours in front of a match burns almost no energy. The author suggests a simple rule: for every hour of watching sport, spend one hour doing it. In this way, you can be a fan and stay healthy at the same time.

title: Looking After Your Health
text:
Good health is more than the absence of illness. Doctors say that it has three parts: physical health, mental health and a healthy lifestyle. Physical health depends on a healthy diet and regular exercise. Mental health means that you can deal with stress, keep friends and enjoy your life. Doctors add that these three parts are connected, so a problem in one of them often affects the others.

Health problems often start slowly. A person who sleeps only five hours a night and eats fast food every day may feel well for years, but after some time the body begins to complain. Experts recommend regular check-ups at a health centre, even when you feel fine, because many illnesses are easier to treat if they are found early.

Governments also play a role. Health care is free in some countries and expensive in others, and this difference can change how long people live. In addition, health and safety rules at work protect employees from accidents. The writer believes that looking after your health is a daily habit, not a short-term project: you should not wait for illness before you take care of yourself.

title: Saving and Spending
text:
Most people earn money, but not everybody knows how to manage it. Financial advisers say that the first rule is simple: spend less than you earn. If you are always short of money at the end of the month, it is useful to write down every expense for a few weeks. Many people are surprised to find how much they waste on small things, such as snacks or things they never use.

The second rule is to save a little regularly. Even a small amount, put aside every month, becomes a useful sum after a few years. It is wise to keep some savings for emergencies, because a broken car or a sudden illness can cost a lot of money. A good habit is to move some money to a separate account on the day when you receive your salary.

Paying by card is now more common than paying in cash. It is convenient, but psychologists warn that people spend more when they do not see the money leave their hand. Children can learn about money early: pocket money teaches them to choose between spending it and saving it. According to the author, the best financial habit is patience.

title: Fresh or Frozen?
text:
Shoppers often believe that fresh food is always healthier than frozen food, but this is not completely true. Fruit and vegetables that are frozen soon after picking can keep most of their vitamins. In contrast, fresh produce that travels for many days to the supermarket may lose some of them. For this reason, a bag of frozen peas can sometimes be a better choice than a tired fresh vegetable.

Fast food and junk food are a bigger problem for our health. Burgers, chips and sweet drinks contain a lot of fat, sugar and salt, and many people eat them several times a week. Doctors say that this habit leads to health problems such as obesity and heart disease. They recommend a healthy diet with plenty of vegetables, whole grains and fish.

There is another trend: organic food, which is produced without most chemicals. It is usually more expensive, and scientists are still discussing whether it is better for our health. Home-cooked food, however, is almost always a good choice, because you decide what goes into the pot. The article concludes that it is not only what we eat that matters, but also how often and how much.

title: Growing Up Online
text:
Today's teenagers are the first generation that has never known a world without the internet. Most of them go online every day: they surf the internet for homework, download music, send messages to friends and play computer games. For many young people, a laptop is as normal as a pen. Some of them even say that the internet is the place where they spend most of their free time.

The internet offers great opportunities. A student in a small village can search for information in a minute and learn a language with a free website. However, there are also dangers. Experts warn that teenagers who spend too many hours on a screen may sleep badly and find it difficult to concentrate. Another problem is online safety: not everybody on the internet is who they say they are.

Parents often ask how much time children should spend online. There is no perfect answer, but many specialists suggest clear rules, for example no phones at dinner and no screens in the bedroom after ten o'clock. title: Planning Around the Weather
text:
Everybody talks about the weather, and for good reason. In many countries, people check the weather before they decide what to wear, where to travel or even what to eat. A reliable weather forecast can save a farmer's crop, help a pilot to choose a safe route and stop a family from holding a picnic on the wrong day.

Different kinds of weather affect our lives in different ways. Terrible weather, such as a heavy storm, can close roads and schools. Wet weather makes outdoor work difficult, and builders often have to stop until the rain ends. Hot weather brings its own problems: it is dangerous for old people, and shops sell out of cold drinks and fans within hours. On the other hand, mild weather is ideal for sport and travel, which is why tourists often visit a country in spring or autumn rather than in the middle of summer.

Forecasters now use satellites and powerful computers, but they still make mistakes. The longer the period, the harder the forecast becomes. A prediction for tomorrow is usually correct, whereas a prediction for next month is little more than a guess. Many people therefore take a coat with them even when the forecast promises sunshine.

title: Living with Noise
text:
Silence is becoming rare in modern cities. Wherever we go, we hear a noise of some kind: traffic, building work, music from a shop or the sound of aeroplanes overhead. Scientists call this background noise, and they believe it is more harmful than most people think.

Researchers in several countries have measured the noise level in different districts. In the busiest streets, it is often as loud as a vacuum cleaner. Residents there sleep badly, and children in nearby schools find it harder to concentrate. A strange noise at night, such as a car alarm, can wake a whole street.

Neighbours are another common problem. Noisy neighbours who play loud music late in the evening cause more arguments than almost anything else in apartment blocks. In some places, the police can fine people if they do not reduce the noise after eleven o'clock.

Fortunately, there are simple solutions. Thick windows keep out most of the traffic sound, and trees along a road can absorb some of it. Some cities have introduced quiet zones near hospitals and parks. The author concludes that silence is not a luxury but a basic need, and that planners should protect it as carefully as clean air.

title: Getting Qualified
text:
Nowadays, it is almost impossible to find a good job without qualifications. Employers want to know that a candidate has the skills for the work, and a certificate is the easiest proof. Students therefore spend years trying to gain a qualification, and many continue studying after they start work.

Different jobs require different qualifications. To qualify as a doctor, a student must study for at least six years and then pass a series of difficult exams. A teaching qualification takes much less time, usually one or two years after university. In some trades, such as plumbing, young people learn on the job and receive a certificate at the end.

However, qualifications alone are not enough. Even if you are qualified for a position, you still have to attend a job interview. Interviewers often ask about your experience, and they pay attention to how you speak and behave. A candidate with the right qualifications but poor communication skills may lose the job to somebody with less training.

title: Pay and Fairness
text:
How much should a worker earn? This question causes more debate than almost any other in politics. In most countries, there is a legal minimum wage, which is the lowest hourly payment an employer is allowed to offer. Supporters say that it protects workers from unfair treatment. Critics argue that it makes small businesses employ fewer people.

There are different ways to be paid. Some people earn a weekly wage, usually calculated by the hour. Others receive a monthly salary, which stays the same even if they work a few extra hours. In most offices, employees expect a salary increase every year, or at least a pay rise when they take on more responsibility.

The differences between jobs can be enormous. A high salary does not always mean an easy life: surgeons, for example, earn a lot, but they work long hours and carry heavy responsibility. A low salary may belong to a job that is useful to everybody, such as a cleaner or a care worker. Many economists admit that the market does not always reward the most valuable work.

For young people choosing a career, the advice is simple. Look at the pay, but also ask whether the work is interesting, and whether you will have the chance to learn.

title: Flight Delays
text:
Few things annoy travellers more than a long delay. A flight may be delayed because of bad weather, a technical fault or a shortage of staff. Sometimes the airline does not apologise for the delay; sometimes it announces a new departure time every half hour, and each announcement makes the passengers angrier.

The passengers' experience depends on their destination and on the length of the delay. A delay of two hours is annoying but bearable, especially if the airport has comfortable seats, cafés and free internet. A delay of ten hours is much worse. Passengers with small children sleep on the floor, and business travellers miss important meetings.

In the European Union, passengers have legal rights. If a flight is cancelled, the airline must offer a new ticket or a refund. In case of very long delays, it must provide food and, if necessary, a hotel room. However, many travellers do not know these rules, and airlines rarely remind them.

Experts recommend that passengers keep calm, take photographs of the departure board and write down the details of every announcement. If a complaint is necessary, evidence like this makes it much easier to win. Most important of all, they say, you should leave home without being in a hurry. Extra time at the airport is better than an extra problem.

title: Packing Light
text:
Every traveller has a luggage story. Some of them are funny, and some are expensive. A man in Spain once arrived at the airport with four huge suitcases and discovered that he had to pay a large fee for excess luggage. A woman travelling to Canada lost her bag and spent three days wearing the same clothes.

Experienced travellers say that the best advice is to pack light. A small bag is easier to carry, and many airlines allow you to take carry-on luggage into the cabin without paying anything. You also avoid the long wait at the baggage belt. Before you leave, make a list of what you need and check in only the items that are really necessary. Heavy or fragile things should go in a hard case, but soft clothes can be rolled and packed in a corner.

Of course, you cannot control everything. Airports sometimes lose your luggage, however carefully you plan. For this reason, travel writers suggest keeping a change of clothes, important medicine and your documents in the cabin bag. It is also sensible to put your name and phone number inside every suitcase, in addition to the label outside.

Finally, remember that you will probably buy something during the trip. Leave some space in your bag, and you will not need a luggage trolley as big as a car.

title: Finding the Way
text:
Before satellite maps, travellers used paper maps and asked local people for directions. Today, most of us follow a route on a phone, and a calm voice tells us where to turn. This is convenient, but it also has disadvantages.

Planning a route is not the same as following one. When you plan a route on a map, you see the whole area and understand how the roads connect. When you follow a voice, you only see the next turn. Researchers have found that drivers who always use electronic navigation remember much less about the places they visit.

The shortest route is not always the best one. A scenic route along the coast may take an hour longer than the main road, but it offers views that many people remember for years. Bus routes in a city are another example. The fastest line may pass through crowded districts, whereas a slower line may be quieter and more comfortable.

Of course, there are times when the phone is the right choice. If you are driving in a strange city at night, it is sensible to follow the instructions carefully. In emergencies, it can save time and even lives.

The author's conclusion is balanced: use technology, but occasionally look at a paper map too. Knowing where you are, not only where to go next, is a skill worth keeping.

title: Exam Season
text:
For many students, the most stressful time of the year is exam season. In May and June, libraries are full, and even the cafés fill with people holding notebooks. Students have to take an exam in every subject, and each result can affect their future.

Teachers advise students to start early. To revise for an exam in a calm way, you should make a timetable and study for short periods, with regular breaks. Reading the whole book the night before is a mistake. Memory works better when information is repeated several times over several weeks.

In many countries, there are two kinds of exam. An entrance exam decides whether you can join a university. A final exam, at the end of a course, shows how much you have learned. Some schools allow you to sit an exam twice if you fail, but others do not.

Of course, marks are not everything. A student who has to pass an exam to enter a medical school will feel the pressure more than somebody who studies for pleasure. Nevertheless, even a student who gets a low mark can learn from it. Teachers say that the exam results should not be seen as a judgement of a person, but as feedback on how well a student prepared.

Above all, they say, do not forget to sleep. A tired student with good notes often does worse than a rested student with fewer.

title: Taking Part
text:
People love competition. Every year, thousands of runners enter a race, even though only a few can win. In a city marathon, the first runner crosses the line in about two hours, while the last may take six hours, but both are proud of what they did.

Races come in many forms. A horse race, a car race and a relay race are completely different, but they have one thing in common: the competitors want to be first. Some races are also a race against time, for example when rescue workers try to save people after an accident.

Competitions are not only about sport. Schools often organise a competition for the best story or the best science project. To win a competition requires hard work, but even those who lose gain experience. Psychologists say that children who take part in competitions learn to deal with disappointment, which is an important life skill.

Not everybody agrees. Some teachers think that too much competition makes weaker students feel useless. They prefer activities in which all students work together and nobody loses. Others reply that life itself is full of competition, so schools should prepare young people for it.

The truth may lie in the middle. A good competition is fair, has clear rules and gives everybody a chance to feel proud. In such a competition, taking part is already a success.

title: Recovering from Illness
text:
Nobody enjoys being ill, but most illnesses are short and minor. A cold, for example, usually lasts a week, and the patient can recover at home with rest and warm drinks. A serious illness, however, changes life more deeply. People who suffer from an illness such as diabetes or heart disease must follow a strict routine for many years.

Doctors say that how quickly we recover depends on several factors. Age is important: young people usually get better faster. Lifestyle matters too. A person who sleeps well and eats healthy food has a stronger body than someone who is tired and stressed. A positive attitude also helps. In several studies, patients who felt hopeful left hospital earlier than those who felt hopeless.

Mental illness deserves special attention. It is common, but it is often hidden because people are afraid of what others will think. A person can catch an illness like flu from a friend, but nobody can catch depression in this way; it has other causes. A mental illness can last a long time, though most people recover with the right help.

Health services therefore encourage everyone to talk openly about how they feel. A short illness is easy to explain. A long illness is harder, and the patient needs friends, patience and understanding.

title: Giving Up Smoking
text:
Most smokers know that smoking is bad for you. Every packet of cigarettes carries a warning, and doctors have repeated the message for decades. Even so, millions of adults continue to smoke cigarettes every day. Why is it so difficult to quit smoking?

The main reason is nicotine, a substance that makes the body want more. After a few weeks, a person feels uncomfortable without it. Many heavy smokers need a cigarette first thing in the morning, and some wake up in the night for one. Habit is another reason. Smokers connect cigarettes with coffee, with breaks at work and with talking to friends.

Meanwhile, the risks become clearer every year. Passive smoking, which means breathing smoke from other people's cigarettes, can harm non-smokers, especially children. For this reason, many countries have created smoke-free areas in restaurants, offices and public transport. In some cities, smoking is banned even in parks.

The good news is that people who give up smoking begin to feel better quickly. Within a few days, breathing is easier, and after a year, the risk of heart disease falls sharply. Experts advise smokers to set a date, ask family for support and avoid situations that bring back the habit.

Giving up is hard, but thousands of people succeed every year. A non-smoker's life is not only longer, but also cheaper.

title: Receiving Treatment
text:
When people become seriously ill, they need treatment, and the type depends on the problem. A broken arm may need only a plaster, whereas a damaged heart may require an operation and several months of care. Doctors usually provide treatment in a hospital, but many patients receive medical treatment at home, especially if the illness is long.

In an emergency, speed is the most important factor. Emergency treatment begins in the ambulance, where trained staff check the patient's breathing and heart. If the patient arrives within an hour, the chances of a full recovery are much higher. For this reason, doctors teach ordinary people basic first aid, so that they can help before the ambulance arrives.

Some diseases still have no complete cure. Doctors can treat the symptoms, but the patient must undergo treatment for years. A course of treatment may last six weeks, six months or longer. Many patients stop too early because they feel better, and this can make the illness return.

Medical research moves quickly, however. Diseases that were once deadly can now be cured with a few tablets. Scientists hope that in the next fifty years, they will find a cure for many more illnesses. Until then, the best advice is simple: see a doctor early, follow the treatment carefully and never stop without asking.

title: Throwing a Party
text:
A good party needs careful planning. If you decide to throw a party, start by choosing the date and making a list of guests. Then think about the place. A small flat can be crowded, so many people prefer to hire a hall or a café for a big event.

Food and music come next. Guests usually expect something to eat and a few drinks, but the host does not have to spend a fortune. A table with sandwiches, fruit and juice is often more popular than an expensive meal. Remember to invite everyone in good time, at least two weeks before, so that they can reserve the date.

Some parties are special. A birthday party is the most common, especially for children, who often play games and receive small gifts. A surprise party needs even more planning, because the guest of honour must not find out. Friends hide in the dark, and when the person enters, everyone shouts "Surprise!" A farewell party, on the other hand, is usually quieter. Colleagues say goodbye to a person who is leaving a job or a town.

Finally, the host should not forget the end of the evening. Ask a friend to help with the cleaning, and thank everyone for coming. A party that ends well is the one that guests remember with pleasure.

title: Making a Film
text:
Many people enjoy watching a film, but few know how much work it takes to make one. Every film begins with an idea. A writer produces a script, often with many changes, and a producer looks for money. Without money, even the best story cannot reach the screen.

When the budget is ready, a director chooses the actors and the places. Some stories are set in a real city; others are shot in a studio, where an artificial street can be built in a few days. Many famous films are based on a book, and fans often complain if the film changes the plot. It is unusual for the film to be better than the book, but it does happen.

The shooting itself may take months. Actors wake up before sunrise and wait for hours in a caravan. When the cameras are finally ready, a single scene may need twenty attempts. To star in a film is exciting, but it is also tiring work.

After shooting, the editor selects the best scenes and joins them together. Then composers add the music, which can change the feeling of a scene. Finally, the film is shown in cinemas, and the producers wait nervously for the first reviews.

For the audience, it is easy to say that a film is bad. For the people who made it, it is more difficult: they know that the result represents years of work.

title: Dress Codes
text:
What we wear tells other people something about us. In many companies, employees have to wear a uniform: a bank clerk wears a suit, a nurse wears a white coat and a waiter wears a black apron. A uniform shows who you are and what your job is.

In other workplaces, the rules are less clear. Some offices ask staff to dress smartly, but they allow casual clothes on Fridays. Newcomers are often unsure what to choose. A good tip is to watch what colleagues do on the first day and then copy them.

Shopping for clothes can be a challenge, too. Before you buy a jacket, you should try it on, because sizes differ from shop to shop. A coat that fits perfectly in one shop may be too tight in another. You should also check whether the colour suits you. A friend's opinion can be valuable.

Fashion changes quickly. Something that is in fashion this year may look strange next year. Some people follow every trend; others prefer simple, classic clothes that never go out of fashion. At a formal event, such as a wedding, guests are often dressed in dark colours, but in some cultures bright clothes are traditional.

In the end, the best advice is to feel comfortable. When you put on a coat or a shirt that you like, you walk differently and speak with more confidence.

title: When Families Separate
text:
Divorce is common in many countries today. In some places, about one marriage in three ends this way. Couples decide to divorce for many reasons, such as arguments about money, different expectations or simply the feeling that they have grown apart.

The legal process varies from country to country. In some places, one partner can file for divorce and wait several months for the court to decide. In others, both partners must agree. After a divorce, the couple usually divides their property and, if there are children, decides where they will live.

Children are the most sensitive part of the story. Psychologists say that a divorced couple can still be good parents if they cooperate. A child needs to hear that the separation is not his or her fault, and needs regular contact with both parents. Problems usually begin when the former partners fight about the children or use them to hurt each other.

Society's attitude has changed. Fifty years ago, a person who got divorced often felt ashamed, and friends avoided the subject. Today, it is accepted as a normal, if painful, event. Support groups, counsellors and even websites help people to start again.

The author concludes that a divorce is neither a disaster nor a solution to every problem. It is a serious decision, and those who make it deserve respect, not judgement.

title: Learning to Control Anger
text:
Everyone feels angry sometimes. You may be angry with a friend who forgot your birthday, or angry about a decision that you think is unfair. Anger itself is a normal emotion. The problem begins when a person cannot control it.

People get angry for different reasons. Some become furious when they are tired or hungry; others react badly to criticism. A noisy room, a long queue or a late bus can make almost anyone angry. In such moments, the body changes: the heart beats faster, the face goes red and the voice becomes louder.

What should you do? Psychologists suggest several steps. First, stop and breathe slowly. Count to ten before you speak. Second, ask yourself whether the problem will matter in a week. If the answer is no, it is not worth losing your temper. Finally, find a calm way to express your feelings. Saying "I feel upset when you are late" is much more useful than shouting.

Some people keep their temper in public but explode at home. This is dangerous for relationships, because family members begin to feel afraid. Exercise can help: a long walk or a game of football often takes away the tension.

If anger affects work or family life, specialists recommend talking to a counsellor. Learning to manage anger is a skill, and like any other skill, it improves with practice.

title: How a Government Works
text:
In a democracy, citizens choose their government by voting in an election. Usually, the election takes place every four or five years. Each party presents its plans, called a programme, and tells voters what it will do if it wins.

After the election, the party with the most votes tries to form a government. If no party has a majority, two or more parties may agree to work together. The leader of the winning party often becomes the prime minister, who then chooses a government minister for each area, such as education, health or transport.

The government has several duties. It prepares the budget, decides how to spend taxes and makes policy on important questions. At the same time, there is local government, which handles daily matters in towns and villages: schools, rubbish collection and street lighting.

Not everyone is satisfied. Critics say that governments make promises before the election and forget them afterwards. In some countries, fewer than half of the citizens vote, because they believe that nothing will change. Experts reply that a low turnout is itself a problem, as the government then represents only part of the people.

The author believes that voting is both a right and a responsibility. Even a single vote can matter, especially in a close election, and people who do not vote lose the chance to be heard.

title: Crime and Punishment
text:
To commit an offence means to break the law. Offences range from minor ones, such as dropping rubbish in the street, to very serious ones, such as robbery. A traffic offence is probably the most common: millions of drivers receive a fine every year for speeding or parking in the wrong place.

How a society reacts depends on the seriousness of the act. For a first offence, a judge may give a warning or order the offender to do community work. For repeated offences, the punishment is stronger, and in the worst cases, the offender goes to prison.

The victim is often forgotten in public discussions. A person whose house has been robbed may feel afraid for months, even if the stolen objects were not valuable. Because of this, some countries have introduced programmes in which the offender meets the victim and apologises. Research shows that victims who take part feel less angry, and that offenders are less likely to repeat the crime.

Not everyone agrees about what punishment is for. Some people say it should protect society by keeping dangerous people away. Others believe it should help offenders to change. A third view is that the penalty should simply match the crime.

The author argues that the most effective approach combines all three ideas. A good system protects the public, treats victims with respect and gives offenders a chance to return to normal life.

title: Languages of the World
text:
There are about seven thousand languages in the world, but half of the population speaks only a few of them. Chinese, English, Hindi and Spanish are used by billions of people. At the same time, many languages have fewer than a thousand speakers, and some are disappearing.

Why do people learn a foreign language? Some do it for work, because employers like candidates who can speak a foreign language. Others do it for travel or for love. Everyone has a mother tongue, which is the first language they learn at home. For many people, it remains the language of emotion: they count, dream and swear in it.

Countries often have one or more official languages. In Switzerland, there are four, and Canadian documents appear in both English and French. A single language can also have many forms. English in Scotland sounds different from English in Australia, although the speakers understand each other.

Learning a language takes time. A language course can give a good start, but real progress needs practice. Experts recommend that learners speak every day, even for ten minutes, and read simple books. Language skills improve more quickly when students are not afraid of mistakes.

Perhaps the most important reason to learn another language is understanding. A person who speaks only one language sees the world in one way; a person who speaks two sees it in at least two. Every new language opens a new door.

title: Giving a Speech
text:
Many people are more afraid of public speaking than of flying. Yet sooner or later almost everyone has to make a speech: at a wedding, at school or at work. The good news is that a speech can be prepared, and preparation makes a big difference.

Start by thinking about your listeners. What do they already know? What do they want to hear? A speech for experts is different from a speech for children. Then write the text. Many speakers write the first sentence and the last sentence word for word, because these are the most important. The middle can be notes.

A short speech is usually better than a long one. An opening speech at a conference lasts five minutes, and a wedding speech should never exceed three. When listeners start to look at their watches, the speaker has already lost them.

When it is time to deliver the speech, speak slowly and look at the audience. Pause after the important points. If you make a mistake, do not apologise too much; just continue. Many speakers use humour, but a joke should be short and not offend anybody.

Practice is the secret. Read the speech aloud at home, or ask a friend to listen. After a few attempts, your voice becomes steady, and your fear becomes much smaller.

As the great speakers know, the goal is not to impress with big words. It is to be understood.
